meta.title: Accounting Case Game — Month-End Close: Missing Accruals
meta.subtitle: Branching, document-driven case simulation
meta.description: Reverse-engineered GameSpec fixture for the month-end-close case of the Next.js Accounting Case Game (src/data/cases/month-end-close/). This is the game agent56-pilot already audits, so the fixture is the direct test of whether GameSpec generalises the pilot's eleven hand-written arithmetic closures into portable assertions.
meta.audience: undergraduate accounting students who have already had the lecture on accruals, prepaids and deferred revenue

objectives.statement: Identify, from an unadjusted trial balance and its supporting schedules, which balances require a period-end adjustment.
objectives.priorInstructionJustification: The case is a post-lecture application exercise; no in-game instruction precedes the first graded decision. Agent 6 rated this "Weak — fine as review, unsuitable as first contact" in agent56-pilot/agent6/records/.

objectives.statement: Record an accrued expense in the period the service was received rather than the period of payment.
Compute and record catch-up amortisation by reconciling a general-ledger prepaid balance to its supporting schedule.
Recognise the earned portion of deferred revenue for the service delivered to date.

derivations.describe: Prepaid D&O catch-up = GL balance less remaining coverage
Deferred revenue earned = 3 contracts x ($15,000 / 12 months)
Total parked in deferred revenue at renewal

artifacts.title: Unadjusted Trial Balance — Nov 30
artifacts.content: Unadjusted trial balance at November 30. Prepaid Expenses $24,000. Accrued Liabilities understated. Deferred Revenue $45,000.

artifacts.title: Vendor Invoice #4821 — IT Services
artifacts.content: Apex IT Solutions, Invoice #4821, $14,200 for cloud infrastructure. Service period November. Received November 28. Not yet approved for payment.

artifacts.title: Prepaid Expense Amortization Schedule
artifacts.content: D&O Insurance. GL balance $24,000. Remaining coverage at Nov 30: one month, $2,000. Amortisation recorded year to date: none.

artifacts.title: Deferred Revenue Memo — Annual Contracts
artifacts.content: Three annual contracts renewed November 1 at $15,000 each. Full $45,000 parked in Deferred Revenue.

artifacts.title: Capital Expenditure Approval — Server Rack
artifacts.content: Server rack capex approval. Already capitalised and depreciating; no period-end adjustment required.

personas.label: Junior Accountant
personas.mission: Close the month without a restatement.

personas.label: Audit Associate
personas.mission: Tie every balance to its supporting schedule.

lines.text: The auditor pulled the deferred revenue rollforward. November revenue is understated. Fix it before the file goes out.

steps.title: Review the Trial Balance
steps.prompt: It's 4:47 PM on November 30. The office is quiet — most of the team left early. You pull up the unadjusted trial balance on your monitor. The controller's sticky note is on your keyboard: "Close by EOD. Don't miss anything." You scan the numbers. Something feels off.

options.label: The Accrued Liabilities balance looks low and Prepaid Expenses may be overstated.
options.feedback: Sharp eye. Both items will need investigation. You advance to the accruals stage.

authority.note: No citable Codification topic. Identifying which balances require period-end adjustment rests on the accrual basis itself, which the Codification assumes rather than states. Naming the honest case is deliberate: forcing an ASC number onto it would be the fabricated-precision failure Agent 5 exists to prevent.

options.label: Only the Accrued Liabilities balance looks off.
options.feedback: You caught one issue but missed the Prepaid overage. Review the prepaid schedule too.

options.label: Everything looks fine — the trial balance is clean.
options.feedback: Not quite. The Accrued Liabilities are understated and Prepaids aren't amortized. Let's dig in.

steps.why: Two accounts are out of line: Accrued Liabilities is understated and Prepaid Expenses was never amortized.

steps.title: Record the Missing Accrual
steps.prompt: You dig into the AP inbox and find it — Invoice #4821 from Apex IT Solutions, $14,200 for cloud infrastructure. Received November 28. Not in the GL. The service happened in November, so the expense belongs here. Your fingers hover over the keyboard. What's the entry?

options.label: Dr. IT Services Expense $14,200 / Cr. Accrued Liabilities $14,200
options.feedback: Correct. The expense belongs in November (period of service). Accrued Liabilities increases.

authority.note: No citable Codification topic. Expense recognition in the period of service rests on the accrual basis itself, which the Codification assumes rather than states. Naming the honest case is deliberate: forcing an ASC number onto it would be the fabricated-precision failure Agent 5 exists to prevent.

options.label: Dr. IT Services Expense $14,200 / Cr. Accounts Payable $14,200
options.feedback: Close — but since the invoice isn't approved for payment yet, Accrued Liabilities is the correct credit, not AP.

options.label: Record it in December when the invoice is paid.
options.feedback: Matching principle: the service was received in November, so the expense is recognized in November.

steps.why: The service was received in November, so the expense is recognised in November.

steps.title: Amortize the Prepaid Expense
steps.prompt: You open the prepaid schedule and your stomach drops. The D&O Insurance hasn't been amortized all year. The GL still shows $24,000 — but only one month of coverage is left. The server rack memo is also in the pile, but a quick check shows that capex is already handled. Focus. What do you adjust?

options.label: Dr. Insurance Expense $22,000 / Cr. Prepaid Insurance $22,000
options.feedback: Exactly right. $24,000 - $2,000 = $22,000 to recognize. The server rack memo was a red herring — that's already handled.

authority.note: No citable Codification topic. Systematic allocation of a prepaid cost over the periods benefited rests on the accrual basis itself, which the Codification assumes rather than states. Naming the honest case is deliberate: forcing an ASC number onto it would be the fabricated-precision failure Agent 5 exists to prevent.

options.label: Dr. Insurance Expense $2,000 / Cr. Prepaid Insurance $2,000
options.feedback: That's only one month's amortization. The schedule shows no amortization was recorded all year — you need to catch up $22,000.

options.label: No adjustment needed — prepaids look fine.
options.feedback: The GL balance of $24,000 vs. a correct balance of $2,000 means $22,000 was never expensed.

steps.why: The GL balance less the remaining coverage is the catch-up amortisation.

steps.title: Recognize Deferred Revenue
steps.prompt: One last item. The deferred revenue memo is sitting in your inbox — three annual contracts renewed November 1, $15,000 each. The full $45,000 is still parked in Deferred Revenue. But November is over. One month of service has been delivered. The auditor's already flagging this account. What do you do?

options.label: Dr. Deferred Revenue $3,750 / Cr. Revenue $3,750
options.feedback: 3 contracts x ($15,000 / 12) = $3,750 for one month of service delivered. Perfect.

authority.note: Revenue from a stand-ready service obligation is recognised over time as the service is delivered.

options.label: Dr. Deferred Revenue $45,000 / Cr. Revenue $45,000
options.feedback: Only one month of service has been delivered. Recognizing the full amount violates the revenue recognition principle.

options.label: Leave Deferred Revenue as-is — it will unwind automatically.
options.feedback: Deferred revenue requires a manual entry each period. Skipping it understates November revenue.

steps.why: One month of a twelve-month obligation has been satisfied on each of three contracts.

content.summaryPassed: Great work — the books are closed and your adjustments were accurate.
content.summaryFailed: The close had some issues. Review the stage breakdown to see where adjustments were missed.

hints.text: Compare the Accrued Liabilities balance to prior months. Does anything seem unusually low?
Check the prepaid balance against the amortization schedule — does it tie?
Remember the matching principle: record expenses in the period the service was received.
The amortization schedule shows what the balance SHOULD be. Subtract from the GL balance to get your adjustment.
Always reconcile GL balances to supporting schedules — the difference is your adjustment.
Each contract is $15,000/year. How much revenue is earned in a single month?
Check the memo: three contracts x monthly rate. Only service delivered to date can be recognized.
No hint. At this seniority the judgement is yours.

assertions.describe: Prepaid D&O catch-up = GL balance - remaining coverage ($24,000 - $2,000)
Deferred revenue earned = 3 contracts x ($15,000 / 12 months)
The parked deferred-revenue balance must tie to contracts x annual value
The accrued invoice amount must appear in the entry the student is graded on
Remaining coverage must be about one month of the annual premium, or the story does not hold together

debrief.headline: Close complete
debrief.body: Four adjustments, four decisions. Review where the points went.
takeaways: An expense belongs to the period of service, not the period of payment.
A GL balance that does not tie to its schedule is the adjustment.
Deferred revenue unwinds by manual entry, one period at a time.
